content.text: Which Australian aeronautical innovation is commonly used to record in-flight data?
Altimeter
Pitot tube
Black box
Transponder
Separate the instruments that measure a flight quantity from the device whose whole purpose is to record data so that it can be examined later.
The Australian contribution to aviation safety was the flight recorder, designed to be crash-protected and beacon-located so that it would survive an accident and be recovered from the wreckage.
C
The black box, that is the flight data recorder - option C.

The flight recorder is the innovation developed in Australia for recording in-flight data. It comprises two independent units: a flight data recorder capturing the essential parameters of the flight (airspeed, altitude, attitude, heading, control positions, engine parameters) and a cockpit voice recorder capturing the crew's voices and radio transmissions. Both are housed in a heavily crash-protected enclosure, are located in the rear of the aircraft where the structure absorbs the impact, and carry an underwater locator beacon, so that the recorded data can be recovered and the flight reconstructed after an accident.

items: A (altimeter) - measures height above the reference level by sensing ambient pressure. It displays a live value to the crew but stores nothing.
B (pitot tube) - measures airspeed from the difference between stagnation and static pressure. Again a live indication only.
D (transponder) - a radio device that identifies the aircraft to air traffic control and replies to interrogation; it transmits the aircraft's identity, not a record of the flight.
1 mark: identifies the black box (flight data recorder) as the correct option

content.text: Which of the following identifies TWO properties of polymers that make them better suited than ceramics for the insulation of telecommunication cables?
Ease of formability and higher density
Ease of formability and higher flexibility
Higher resistance to abrasion and higher density
Higher resistance to abrasion and higher flexibility

Cable insulation must be extruded or coated continuously over a long length of conductor, and it must survive installation bending and movement afterwards. Compare FORMABILITY and FLEXIBILITY rather than strength.

Test each option by asking whether BOTH properties claimed are genuine advantages of polymers over ceramics in this application. Any option containing a property that is not an advantage, or that polymers do not actually gain, must be rejected.
B
Ease of formability and higher flexibility - option B.

Polymers such as polyethylene and PVC are viscoelastic: they soften when hot and can be extruded continuously, coated or moulded over long lengths of conductor in a single continuous production run, and they bond tightly to the conductor jacket. This formability is what allows economical mass production of cable. The finished insulation is also compliant, so it conforms to the conductor, allows the cable to be bent and coiled during installation, and tolerates thermal expansion and movement in the ground without cracking.
Ceramics, by contrast, are hard, stiff and brittle with essentially no plastic deformation available, so they cannot be extruded over a cable at all and would fracture if the cable were bent.

items: A (ease of formability and higher density) - higher density is not an advantage of polymers over ceramics for insulation, so this pairing cannot be the reason.
C (higher resistance to abrasion and higher density) - again contains higher density, and abrasion resistance is not what distinguishes the two classes for insulation.

D (higher resistance to abrasion and higher flexibility) - flexibility is correct, but abrasion resistance is not a reason to prefer polymers here; ceramics have good abrasion resistance, and the working cable is not rubbing against anything.
1 mark: selects ease of formability and higher flexibility

content.text: Which AND gate shows the correct output for its given inputs?

content.alt_text: AND gate option A: inputs 0 V and 0 V, output 5 V
content.caption: Option A: 0 V and 0 V in, 5 V out

content.alt_text: AND gate option B: inputs 5 V and 5 V, output 0 V
content.caption: Option B: 5 V and 5 V in, 0 V out

content.alt_text: AND gate option C: inputs 0 V and 5 V, output 5 V
content.caption: Option C: 0 V and 5 V in, 5 V out

content.alt_text: AND gate option D: inputs 5 V and 5 V, output 5 V
content.caption: Option D: 5 V and 5 V in, 5 V out

content.text: An AND gate's output is ON only when EVERY input is ON. Write the truth table for two inputs, row by row, before looking at the options.
Using $5\,\mathrm{V}$ for logic 1 and $0\,\mathrm{V}$ for logic 0, test each option's stated output against that rule. Exactly one row of the truth table produces a high output.
D

For two inputs the AND truth table is $0\cdot0 \to 0$, $0\cdot1 \to 0$, $1\cdot0 \to 0$ and $1\cdot1 \to 1$. So the only correct case is $5\,\mathrm{V}$ and $5\,\mathrm{V}$ in, giving $5\,\mathrm{V}$ out - option D.

items: A ($0\,\mathrm{V}$ and $0\,\mathrm{V}$ in, $5\,\mathrm{V}$ out) - both inputs are logic 0, so an AND gate must output $0\,\mathrm{V}$. A high output with both inputs low is the behaviour of a NOT (or an OR) gate.

B ($5\,\mathrm{V}$ and $5\,\mathrm{V}$ in, $0\,\mathrm{V}$ out) - both inputs are logic 1, so an AND gate must output $5\,\mathrm{V}$. A low output with both inputs high is the behaviour of a NAND gate.
C ($0\,\mathrm{V}$ and $5\,\mathrm{V}$ in, $5\,\mathrm{V}$ out) - one input is low, so the AND output must be $0\,\mathrm{V}$. A high output with only one input high is the behaviour of an OR gate.
D ($5\,\mathrm{V}$ and $5\,\mathrm{V}$ in, $5\,\mathrm{V}$ out) - both inputs are logic 1, so the AND output is $5\,\mathrm{V}$. Correct.
1 mark: selects the gate whose output is the logical AND of its inputs ($5\,\mathrm{V}$ and $5\,\mathrm{V}$ gives $5\,\mathrm{V}$)

content.text: A general purpose bolt drawn to AS 1100 drawing standards is shown.

content.alt_text: General purpose bolt drawn to AS 1100 with dimensions 50, 36 and 7
content.caption: Bolt with dimensions 50, 36 and 7

content.text: What is the diameter of the bolt?
$8.75\,\mathrm{mm}$
$10.00\,\mathrm{mm}$
$14.00\,\mathrm{mm}$
$18.00\,\mathrm{mm}$

Do not measure the drawing - use the standard. AS 1100 fixes the proportions of a general purpose hexagon head bolt as fixed multiples of the nominal diameter $d$, and one of the three dimensions given is governed by one of those ratios.
Decide which of the three dimensions is a fixed proportion of $d$ and which are chosen from a preferred-length list, then divide that dimension by its standard ratio to obtain $d$.

Sanity-check the result against the other two dimensions - the head width across flats and the overall bolt length are also standard multiples of $d$, so a candidate diameter should make the other two dimensions sensible too.
B
The $7\,\mathrm{mm}$ dimension is the hexagon head thickness. AS 1100 gives head thickness $= 0.7d$, so $d = 7/0.7 = 10\,\mathrm{mm}$.

items: 1 mark: applies the AS 1100 head-thickness relationship and selects $10.00\,\mathrm{mm}$

content.text: Using computer-aided drawing (CAD) software a new outline was produced $18.32\,\mathrm{mm}$ away from the original outline of an item as shown.

content.alt_text: Solid original outline with a parallel dashed new outline offset from it, labelled New outline and Original outline, NOT TO SCALE
content.caption: Original outline with a parallel offset new outline

content.text: Which CAD command can produce this result most efficiently?
Trim
Offset
Mirror
Expand

Both outlines are exactly the same shape and the same size - only the position has changed. Look for the CAD command whose defining feature is a copy of an object generated automatically at a constant perpendicular distance from the original, with the distance entered once as a single value.
A useful check: the command must work on a whole closed outline (however many segments it contains), not on a single line, and it must not scale, reflect or shorten the original object.
B

Offset creates a new object that is a constant distance from an existing object, measured perpendicular to it, and it does this along the whole length of the object from a single entered distance of $18.32\,\mathrm{mm}$ - exactly the result shown.

items: Trim cuts away the part of an object lying beyond an intersection line; it deletes material rather than copying the outline, so nothing new can appear at a set distance.
Mirror reflects the object about a chosen axis, producing a reversed copy at an angle, not a parallel copy at a measured distance.
Expand enlarges an object by a scale factor about its centre, so the copy would be a different size as well as a different position.
1 mark: identifies Offset as the command that creates a parallel copy at a set distance

content.text: The schematic diagram shows a bridge rectifier.

content.alt_text: Bridge rectifier schematic with four diodes, an AC source and positive output terminal
content.caption: Bridge rectifier with four diodes and an AC source

content.text: What is the function of this bridge rectifier?
To increase voltage
To decrease voltage
To convert DC to AC
To convert AC to DC

The four diodes are connected so that a different pair conducts on each half of the AC cycle. Trace the current through the load for the positive half cycle and then for the negative half cycle, and ask which way it flows through the load each time.
D

Two diodes conduct on each half cycle and each conduction pair drives current through the load in the same direction, so the pulses always run the same way through the output terminal. This is full-wave rectification: the alternating supply is converted into a unidirectional (DC) output, which is why the circuit is drawn with a positive output terminal.

items: Options A and B (increase or decrease voltage) describe a transformer or a series/parallel arrangement of sources; no diode arrangement changes the magnitude of the voltage in this way.
Option C (DC to AC) describes an inverter, which needs an oscillator and a switching device, not a passive diode network.
1 mark: identifies that the bridge rectifier converts AC to DC

assets.caption: Bridge rectifier with four diodes and an AC source

content.text: A box sits on a horizontal surface. The box begins to slip when this surface is tilted to $28^{\circ}$. What is the coefficient of friction between the box and the surface?
At the instant the box is about to slip, the friction force has reached its limiting value $F = \mu N$, and it is this that balances the component of the weight acting down the incline.
Write the two equations of equilibrium for the box - one perpendicular to the surface and one parallel to it - and eliminate the normal reaction $N$ to leave only the angle and $\mu$.
C
At the point of slipping $\mu = \tan\theta = \tan 28^{\circ} = 0.532$.

items: 1 mark: correct numerical coefficient of friction, $0.532$

content.text: Which row of the table correctly identifies the routine maintenance responsibilities of an aeronautical engineer working for a small commercial airline?
Design of modifications: ✕; Construction of prototypes: ✕; Certification of repairs: ✓; Supervision of maintenance: ✓
Design of modifications: ✓; Construction of prototypes: ✕; Certification of repairs: ✕; Supervision of maintenance: ✓
Design of modifications: ✓; Construction of prototypes: ✓; Certification of repairs: ✕; Supervision of maintenance: ✕
Design of modifications: ✕; Construction of prototypes: ✓; Certification of repairs: ✓; Supervision of maintenance: ✕

Sort each column into two groups: work that belongs to an aircraft manufacturer or design organisation, and work that belongs to the operator who keeps aircraft flying. A small airline keeps its own aircraft serviceable; it does not build prototypes.
Watch for the row that ticks a design activity together with a maintenance activity - only one of those two can belong to an airline's own engineering function.
A

An airline's engineering function exists to keep the aircraft it operates airworthy: it inspects and services them, repairs defects, certifies the work that has been carried out and supervises the licensed maintenance personnel who do it. Designing modifications requires design authority held by the manufacturer, and building prototypes belongs to the manufacturer's design and development work, so neither of those columns can be ticked for an airline engineer.
The correct row therefore ticks certification of repairs and supervision of maintenance only.

items: 1 mark: selects the row with certification of repairs and supervision of maintenance ticked

content.text: A sketch of a post-tensioned concrete beam is shown.

content.alt_text: Pictorial sketch of a post-tensioned concrete beam labelled Front
content.caption: Pictorial sketch of a post-tensioned concrete beam

content.text: Which of the following shows the most likely loading condition the beam is designed to resist when viewed from the front?

content.alt_text: Loading condition A: two upward end loads and one upward mid-span load on the beam viewed from the front
content.caption: Option A

content.alt_text: Loading condition B: two upward end loads and one downward mid-span load
content.caption: Option B

content.alt_text: Loading condition C: three upward loads along the beam
content.caption: Option C

content.alt_text: Loading condition D: one downward mid-span load and two upward end loads
content.caption: Option D: downward mid-span load with upward end reactions, i.e. hogging

content.text: Mark the tendons on the sketch. Before any service load is applied, jacking and anchoring the tendons has already put the whole section into compression - that is the whole point of post-tensioning.

So ask which loading the member is proportioned for: the applied load acts between the supports, and the supports push back up on the member. Rule out any option whose three force arrows could not balance, and rule out the option that pulls the ends down and pushes the middle up, which is the reverse of the stress pattern the tendons create.
D

A post-tensioned member is cast in place and then stressed by tendons that are anchored only at the ends, so the tendons act along the length of the beam and keep the concrete in compression across the whole depth when the service load is applied. The beam is therefore proportioned for a load applied between its supports with the supports supplying upward reactions - in the front view, one load acting downward at mid-span with the two end reactions acting upward.

The option with all three arrows pointing the same way cannot represent a beam in equilibrium, and the option with downward end loads and an upward mid-span load is a hogging condition - the reverse of the compression the tendons are there to provide.

items: 1 mark: selects D - the sagging, simply supported condition (applied load acting down at mid-span with both support reactions acting up), which is the loading a post-tensioned beam is proportioned for; no mark for A (hogging: both end loads down, mid-span arrow up), B or C (three arrows that cannot balance).

content.text: The diagram shows the airflow in a venturi.

content.alt_text: Venturi tube with airflow left to right, narrow throat, and pressure gauges P1 upstream and P2 at the throat
content.caption: Venturi tube with pressure gauges P1 and P2

content.text: What does this diagram illustrate?
Coriolis effect
Pascal’s principle
Dynamic pressure
Bernoulli’s principle

The tube narrows, so the same mass of air per second has to move faster at the throat. Decide what must happen to the pressure there for the air to be able to speed up in the way the continuity equation requires.
Air is a fluid in steady motion, so the energy per unit volume of the air is unchanged along the tube: any increase in kinetic energy must be paid for by a drop in static pressure.
D

content.latex: A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad v_2 > v_1 \ \ \text{because}\ A_2 < A_1
p_1 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_1^{2} = p_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v_2^{2} \quad\Rightarrow\quad p_2 < p_1

content.text: Continuity forces the air to accelerate through the throat, and conservation of energy requires the static pressure to fall by the same amount that the kinetic energy rises. A pressure difference between the wide and narrow parts of a flowing fluid is Bernoulli's principle, and a venturi is one of its standard applications (the same effect drives a carburettor and a sprayer).

items: Pascal's principle applies to a confined fluid at rest, not to a fluid that is flowing through a constriction.

Dynamic pressure $q = \tfrac{1}{2}\rho v^{2}$ is a property of the flow at a point, not the pressure difference between two gauges, and it is a component of the Bernoulli equation rather than an alternative to it.
The Coriolis effect only arises in a rotating frame of reference, such as the Earth's rotation.
1 mark: identifies Bernoulli’s principle (pressure difference in a flowing fluid)

content.text: The table shows materials that have been used to build civil structures over time. Which row of the table shows the use of the materials in the correct historical order?
Earliest: Stone; : Cast iron; : Alloy steel
Earliest: Wrought iron; : Stone; : Alloy steel
Earliest: Timber; : Stainless steel; : Mild steel
Earliest: Cast iron; : Stainless steel; : Mild steel

Date each material before you read the rows: stone and timber are prehistoric, wrought iron belongs to the Iron Age, cast iron to about the 1700s, mild steel to the 1850s, stainless steel to about 1913, and alloy steels are 20th century.
Then read each row strictly from left to right as earliest to latest and reject any row in which a material appears before one that was actually used earlier.
A

items: Row A - stone, cast iron, alloy steel: stone structures are prehistoric, cast iron came into structural use in the 1700s and alloy steels are 20th century, so the dates increase all the way along the row.
Row B - wrought iron, stone, alloy steel: fails immediately, because stone was being built with thousands of years before wrought iron was worked.
Row C - timber, stainless steel, mild steel: the last two are reversed, since mild steel dates from the 1850s (Bessemer process) and stainless steel only from about 1913.
Row D - cast iron, stainless steel, mild steel: also reverses mild steel and stainless steel, so it cannot be correct either.

content.text: Only the first row lists the materials in the order in which they were actually used to build civil structures.

items: 1 mark: selects the row that orders the materials correctly from earliest to latest

content.text: Which row of the table indicates the effects of retrofitting winglets to a plane?
Lift: Decreases; Drag: Decreases; Vortices: Decrease
Lift: Increases; Drag: Decreases; Vortices: Decrease
Lift: Decreases; Drag: Increases; Vortices: Increase
Lift: Increases; Drag: Increases; Vortices: Increase

A wingtip is the source of the trailing vortex - high-pressure air flows around the tip from below to the low-pressure region above, and the swirl that creates costs lift as induced drag. Think about what a small vertical surface placed at the tip does to that flow.
Follow the consequences through: if less lift is being lost to the tip vortex, what happens to the lift the wing can generate at a given speed, and to the drag the aircraft has to overcome?
B

Winglets act as small end plates. By obstructing the spanwise flow around the tip they weaken the trailing vortex, which reduces the induced drag the aircraft has to overcome. With induced drag reduced, the wing can generate the lift needed to hold the weight at a smaller angle of attack, so the total lift available at a given speed and angle of attack increases.

items: The row with lift decreasing is wrong because reducing the induced drag increases the lift the wing can produce, it does not reduce it.
The two rows with drag and vortices increasing are the opposite of the effect a wingtip device has; a wingtip surface is fitted precisely to reduce the tip vortices, not to strengthen them.
1 mark: selects increased lift with decreased drag and decreased vortices

questions.notes: Stored key C (0.80) corrected to B. Official NESA 2019 Section I answer key gives Q13 = B (0.75). 0.80 is only the mass ratio 20/25; the velocity ratio from the two 2 m arms is 1.0 and MA = efficiency x VR = 0.75 × 1.0 = 0.75.

content.text: The diagram shows a seesaw being used by two children, one of mass $25\,\mathrm{kg}$ and the other of mass $20\,\mathrm{kg}$. It has a corroded pivot mechanism that reduces its efficiency by $25\%$.

content.alt_text: Seesaw on a central pivot with a 25 kg child 2 m from the pivot and a 20 kg child 2 m from the pivot on the other side
content.caption: Seesaw with 25 kg and 20 kg children 2 m either side of the pivot

content.text: What is the mechanical advantage of the seesaw?
Mechanical advantage is not the ratio of the two children's masses. Use the relationship between the three machine quantities, $\eta = \dfrac{MA}{VR}$, and start with the velocity ratio.

The velocity ratio comes from the geometry - the distance the effort moves compared with the distance the load moves - and the $25\%$ loss then reduces the mechanical advantage below that geometric value.
B

Both children sit the same distance from the pivot, so for every millimetre the $20\,\mathrm{kg}$ child moves down the other end moves up by the same amount and the velocity ratio of the seesaw is $1.0$. The corroded pivot is $25\%$ lossy, so the seesaw as it actually operates has a mechanical advantage of only $75\%$ of that: $MA = 0.75$. In practice the seesaw therefore cannot quite overcome the difference between the two children - an ideal one would balance, this one tips towards the $25\,\mathrm{kg}$ child.
The value $0.80$ is just the ratio of the two masses, $20/25$; it is a property of the children, not of the machine, and it ignores both the equal arms and the stated efficiency.

items: 1 mark: correct mechanical advantage, $0.80$

questions.notes: Stored key B corrected to A. Official NESA 2019 Section I answer key gives Q14 = A. In the Australian 625-line PAL-B/G analogue system the vision carrier is AM and the sound carrier is FM, so 'FM signals used to transmit audio' is the correct pairing; the stored key had applied AM to the audio.

content.text: Which row of the table correctly identifies key features of analogue and digital signals used in the transmission of television in Australia?
Analogue television signals: FM signals used to transmit audio; Digital television signals: MP2 or MP4 compression used to transmit video
Analogue television signals: AM signals used to transmit audio; Digital television signals: MP2 or MP4 compression used to transmit video
Analogue television signals: FM signals used to transmit luminescence; Digital television signals: VOIP used to transmit video
Analogue television signals: AM signals used to transmit luminescence; Digital television signals: VOIP used to transmit video

Australian analogue television used the 625-line PAL-B/G system. Decide for that system which carrier was amplitude modulated and which was frequency modulated, and whether the modulated carrier carries the picture or the sound.

For the digital column, check what is actually applied to the video before it is transmitted, and reject any cell that describes the picture by an optical term or claims that video is sent as a voice call.
A

In the PAL-B/G system used in Australia the vision (picture) carrier is amplitude modulated and the sound is carried on a separate frequency-modulated carrier, so the analogue column must read FM with audio. Digital television applies MPEG-2 (and later MPEG-4) compression to the video before transmission, so that part of the row is correct in every option.

items: Option B pairs AM with the audio, which is the system used where the sound is transmitted as an AM intercarrier - not the Australian system.

Options C and D describe the picture as 'luminescence', which is not a term used for the television signal, and both claim the video is sent by VOIP, a voice-only technique that carries speech, not compressed pictures.

content.text: The row that pairs FM audio with MP2/MP4 video compression is therefore the correct one.

items: 1 mark: selects the row pairing AM audio with MP2/MP4 compressed video

content.text: Titanium is used to manufacture aircraft undercarriages that support landing wheels. Why is titanium used in preference to alloy steel for this purpose?
It has lower density and lower strength.
It has lower density and higher strength.
It has higher density and lower strength.
It has higher density and higher strength.

The undercarriage has to carry the same landing load whichever material it is made from, so compare the materials on mass carried per unit of strength rather than on strength alone. Use the strength-to-weight ratio, $\sigma \div \rho$.
Two of the four options make the titanium heavier than steel, which can never be a reason for choosing it, so those can be discarded before comparing strengths.
B

Aluminium-lithium and titanium alloys are used for undercarriages and landing gear because they are far lighter than steel for a comparable load-carrying capability, giving a much higher strength-to-weight ratio. A lighter undercarriage reduces the mass the airframe must carry and the energy the structure has to absorb on impact, and titanium also resists the corrosion that salt spray causes. Only one option pairs the lower density with the higher strength, which is the required combination.

items: 1 mark: identifies lower density combined with higher strength

content.text: The image shows part of a large anchor recovered from waters off Western Australia. The anchor’s approximate date of manufacture was $1790$.

content.alt_text: Photograph of part of a large wrought iron anchor recovered from waters off Western Australia
content.caption: Photograph of part of a large anchor

content.text: This anchor is most likely made from
cast iron.
cast steel.
wrought iron.
laminated silicon steel.

Use the date. Compare $1790$ with the period in which each material became available in quantity for large forged structural work, and remember that a ship's anchor must survive being dragged over a seabed and struck hard by the hull.
One option is a brittle material that is strong in compression but will not tolerate impact tension, and one option is a modern laminated electrical steel that did not exist at all in the 1790s.
C

Wrought iron - low-carbon iron worked by forging and welding - was the standard material for anchors, chain and ship's fittings from the Iron Age until the middle of the 19th century, and an anchor dated to about $1790$ would be wrought iron forged from bar stock. Cast iron, although used for cookware and later for columns, is brittle and would fracture under the shock of a ship dragging it, and cast steel and laminated silicon steel both post-date the anchor by a century or more.

items: 1 mark: identifies wrought iron as the material consistent with a 1790 manufacture date

Lead alloy battery plates: Cold rolling; Steel body panels: Cold rolling
Lead alloy battery plates: Cold rolling; Steel body panels: Hot rolling
Lead alloy battery plates: Hot rolling; Steel body panels: Cold rolling
Lead alloy battery plates: Hot rolling; Steel body panels: Hot rolling

Start with the steel body panel. Cold rolling is worked below the recrystallisation temperature, so the sheet comes out accurate in thickness, work-hardened and with a smooth surface that can be painted; hot rolling is done above that temperature for thick plate and heavy sections. Which does a vehicle body panel need?
Having settled the body panel, use the second column to find the remaining row and read the lead alloy cell off that row.
C

Hot and cold rolling are separated by the recrystallisation temperature, not by the melting point. Cold rolling is worked below the recrystallisation temperature, so the metal work-hardens and comes out with an accurate gauge and a high quality surface finish; hot rolling is worked above it, where the metal is soft and ductile.

A vehicle body panel has to be thin, accurately gauged and have a finish that can be painted, so the steel body panels are cold rolled. That immediately rules out both rows that put hot rolling on the panels.

In the remaining rows the lead alloy cell is hot rolled. Lead melts at $327^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ but is nowhere near that temperature when it is rolled, and its recrystallisation temperature is at about room temperature, so a lead alloy plate rolled at room temperature is being hot worked. That is what the question's phrase 'at room temperature' is testing.
The keyed row is therefore hot rolling for the lead alloy battery plates and cold rolling for the steel body panels, which is option C.

items: 1 mark: selects option C - hot rolling for the lead alloy battery plates and cold rolling for the steel body panels

content.text: What is the energy stored in this shock absorber?
$12\,\mathrm{J}$
$36\,\mathrm{J}$
$48\,\mathrm{J}$
$120\,\mathrm{J}$
Energy stored is the work done by the average force acting through the distance the shock absorber actually shortens by - that distance is the change in length, not the length it started at.

Careful with the $\tfrac{1}{2}Fd$ form of the energy equation: it applies when $F$ is the final (maximum) force. Here the $400\,\mathrm{N}$ is stated as an average, so multiply it by the full change in length.
A

The shock absorber is compressed by $30\,\mathrm{mm}$, and the work done in compressing it is the average force multiplied by that compression, giving $12\,\mathrm{J}$ stored in the compressed gas and springs. Because the force quoted is an average, the $\tfrac{1}{2}Fd$ form (which would give $6\,\mathrm{J}$) does not apply here.

The distractor $48\,\mathrm{J}$ is obtained by multiplying the average force by the uncompressed length, $400 \times 0.120$: the shock absorber does no work over that distance, because the piston has not moved until the compression starts.

$135.0\,\mathrm{MPa}$
$136.4\,\mathrm{MPa}$
$150.0\,\mathrm{MPa}$

Engineering stress is always calculated on the original cross-sectional area, whatever the specimen has done since. True stress is the load divided by the area that is actually carrying the load at that instant.

content.text: The design of this bus shelter includes the use of toughened glass panels. Outline advantages of using toughened glass for this bus shelter.
Think about what happens when a pane of glass in a bus shelter is struck or overloaded. The strongest answer describes how the panel fails, not just how strong it is.
Also consider how the panel survives cleaning, handling and installation, and how the behaviour of the fragments affects the people waiting underneath it.
Give several distinct advantages, each as a property linked to the service condition, so that each earns its own mark.

items: High in flexural strength, so a thin panel can span the shelter openings and resist wind loading.
Breaks into smaller, safer pieces when broken by an applied load, reducing the risk of serious injury to people using the shelter.
Strong edge strength, which resists chipping during transport and installation, so the panel keeps its full strength in service.
Harder and more scratch resistant than annealed glass, so routine cleaning and graffiti removal do not degrade it.

content.text: A laminated timber beam is used as part of the roof construction for this bus shelter. Apart from cost and aesthetics, justify why laminated timber would be selected for this structure.
The question says 'apart from cost and aesthetics', so every justification must be about performance, durability or form.
Think about what a laminated section can be made to do that a solid timber beam of the same span cannot: consider the shapes and the sizes that natural timber does not come in.
Then consider the adhesive layers between the laminations and what service environments they tolerate.

items: Laminated timber can be made to any desired shape or size, so the roof beam can be formed to the required shape and span the shelter without joints.
The synthetic adhesives used to bond the laminates have a resistance to chemical and acid attack, so the beam retains its strength and bond integrity in an outdoor, exposed position.
Defects and knots can be cut out of the laminations, giving a stronger and more rigid beam than solid timber of the same size.
A better strength-to-weight ratio than a comparable steel member, and improved fire resistance, both of which reduce the load carried by the supporting structure.

content.text: Describe a testing procedure that could be used to determine the structural strength of the laminated timber beam. Support your answer with a labelled sketch.
The quantity being sought is the structural strength of the beam in bending, which points to a flexural (bending) test rather than a tensile, compressive or impact test.
Plan the test as a sequence: mark out a span on the beam, set it up on supports, decide where the load is applied, increase the load, and record both the load and the resulting deflection.
Your sketch must carry the information a marker needs: the two supports, the span, the single or double point of load application with the load arrow, and the deflection measurement.

items: A transverse bend test (three-point flexural test) is used, because it measures the flexural strength of the beam.
Measure and mark a span on the beam, then support it at each end on a simple support and a roller so the beam cannot move horizontally.
Apply a single point load at mid-span with the ram of a universal testing machine, or a double point load, at a constant rate.
Measure the deflection at the load point with a dial gauge at fixed load increments, or record deflection continuously while the load increases.
Plot load against deflection. The gradient of the initial straight portion is the flexural stiffness, and the maximum load reached before failure is the flexural (structural) strength of the beam.
Support the procedure with a labelled sketch showing the supports, the span, the load application point(s) and the deflection measurement.

content.text: Explain why the engineer has positioned the repeater transmitters as indicated on the diagram.

The marks are for the consequence of separating those paths (less interference, stronger signal, greater range), not for a description of the physical structure of the tower or its supports.

A repeater receives a weak signal and re-transmits it, so it relies on a clear line-of-sight path. That gives moments about C of $3(18) + 12(4) + 7(10) = 172$ over a 12 m arm, so $R_A = 14.33$ kN; the roller at A forces $F_{AC} = 0$ by horizontal equilibrium at the joint, and $N = R_A = 14.33$ kN in compression, which confirms the keyed value exactly. For M, joint C gives $F_{CE} = 4.67/\sin 71.6^{\circ} = 4.92$ kN compression and $F_{BC} = 3 + 4.92\cos 71.6^{\circ} = 4.56$ kN tension, and the section BD / BE / DE with moments about D, on a moment arm for M of $BD\sin 40.6^{\circ} = 4.12$ m, gives $F_M = [14.33(2) - 4.56(6)]/4.12 = 0.324$ kN in tension - the keyed value again. Note that F and H are not dimensioned in the figure, but neither result depends on F's position, because both are fixed by the reaction and by the joints at A, C and B. content.text: By considering any necessary reaction, calculate the magnitude of the forces in members M and N. State the nature of each force. Ignore the weight of the tower.
Start with the supports: where a support reaction has no horizontal component, the member in line with that direction is a redundant (zero-force) member and can be ignored at that joint.

Find the remaining reaction from moments about a joint where the unknown reaction does not appear, then cut the truss through three members and take moments about the joint where the other two cross, so that only one unknown is left in the equation.
Decide tension or compression from the sense of the moment the assumed force produces, not from the size of the number.
Member $N$: $14.33\,\mathrm{kN}$ in compression. Member $M$: $0.324\,\mathrm{kN}$ in tension.

Reactions. Take moments about C, the pin, where both components of the reaction pass. Measured from the printed figure: the 3 kN horizontal load acts at H, 18 m above C; the 12 kN load acts at G, 4 m to the left of C; the 7 kN load acts at D, 10 m to the left of C; and the roller reaction acts at A, 12 m to the left of C. Those two horizontal distances are exactly the printed 4 m and 2 m dimensions used as moment arms - D lies 2 m to the right of the A/B line and C is 12 m from it - together with the printed 12 m span.

Member N. At joint A the support is a roller, so the reaction there is vertical only. Member AB (N) runs vertically and member AC is inclined, so horizontal equilibrium at that joint can only be satisfied by $F_{AC} = 0$: AC is a redundant (zero-force) member for this loading. Vertical equilibrium then puts the whole reaction into AB, and a compressed AB pushes down on the joint to balance the reaction pushing up, so:

Member M. First the force in BC, from joint C. With AC carrying nothing and the leg CE inclined at $71.6^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, vertical equilibrium of the joint gives the leg and horizontal equilibrium then gives the bottom chord:

Now cut the truss through BD, BE (member M) and DE and take moments about D, where BD and DE intersect, so that only M is left in the equation. The perpendicular distance from D to the line of BE is $BD\sin 40.6^{\circ} = \sqrt{2^{2} + 6^{2}} \times \sin 40.6^{\circ} = 6.32 \times 0.651 = 4.12\,\mathrm{m}$; the printed $40.6^{\circ}$ is the angle between BD and BE, which is the printed $71.6^{\circ}$ less the printed $31^{\circ}$. The vertical force in AB works on a 2 m arm about D and the horizontal force in BC on a 6 m arm:

The sense settles the tension/compression question: the force in BE has to act along BE away from B for the moment equation to close, and a member can only pull a joint towards its far node in tension.

This replaces a defective stored version of the working. It read '$BH = 182 + 62 = 360$ and $d = 360\sin 40.6^{\circ} = 12.348\,\mathrm{m}$', and neither step is arithmetic: $182 + 62$ is $244$, not $360$, and $360\sin 40.6^{\circ}$ is $234.9$, not $12.348$. The figure $12.348$ is in fact the perpendicular distance from joint H to the line of BE, since $BH = \sqrt{18^{2} + 6^{2}} = 18.97\,\mathrm{m}$ and $18.97\sin 40.6^{\circ} = 12.35\,\mathrm{m}$, so the number is sound but the expression printed with it is not. Even so a section cutting BE together with the two leg members is not a valid three-member cut in this truss, because the diagonal DG crosses the same line, and taking moments about H for the portion above such a cut gives $24 = 12.348\,F_M$, i.e. $F_M = 1.94\,\mathrm{kN}$ rather than the keyed $0.324\,\mathrm{kN}$. The section and moment centre used above do reproduce the official values exactly, from the printed dimensions and angles alone.

content.text: How can engineers use an understanding of the effects of drag to improve the design of racing yacht hulls?
Drag opposes forward motion, so reducing it lets the same power drive the boat faster. Start from that link, because the question asks how an understanding of drag improves the design.
A hull drags in two ways: skin friction over its wetted surface, and pressure drag from the low pressure in the separated wake. Ask which of the two each design change reduces.
The appendages under a racing hull are not decoration — use the diagram to identify where the water is deflected and how that reduces the wake.

A hull is a bluff body at the bow: the flow separates at the shoulders and leaves a large low-pressure turbulent wake, so pressure drag is high. Engineers reduce it by giving the hull a fine, rounded entry that keeps the flow attached, a long straight tapering run aft that delays separation and shrinks the wake, a slim underwater form with low wetted area to cut skin-friction drag, and a smooth polished surface to reduce friction further. Appendages such as a keel, bulb or canting foil create a lift-induced deflected flow that reduces the wake. Because drag opposes motion, less drag means less power for a given speed, so the boat reaches a higher speed.
Minimised drag means maximum forward thrust hence increased speed; polished surfaces minimise drag; and a streamlined hull shape minimises vortices.

content.text: Some materials have properties that allow them to be used in the manufacture of both modern racing yachts and aircraft. These materials include Kevlar® aramid fibre, carbon fibre epoxy composites and aluminium alloys. Complete the table by providing a property which makes each of these materials suitable for the manufacture of both yachts and aircraft.

Use the property a student would be asked to justify a composite or an alloy with — specific strength or specific stiffness — rather than a vague claim that it is strong or light.
Keep the same standard of justification in all three rows; a good answer in one row does not carry the others.

rows: Very high specific strength (high tensile strength at very low mass), and it is tough and tear resistant, so it absorbs impact and vibration without splitting in a hull or an airframe panel.
Very high specific stiffness and strength with good fatigue resistance, so it holds its shape under load at minimum mass and does not need thick sections.

content.text: Explain why engineers use CAD software to design and model intricate components.
The question asks why, so link each CAD capability to a consequence for the designer: accuracy, speed of change, sharing, and analysis.
Compare modelling in CAD with producing the same part by hand or as a physical prototype — the argument is about what becomes possible or cheaper, not about what the software is.
Remember that a model can be analysed and tested on screen before any material is cut, and that one parametric file can be used by a whole team and reused for every derived drawing.

CAD allows intricate, complex shapes — some of which cannot be produced by conventional methods — to be modelled, drawn and dimensioned accurately and far more quickly than by hand. The model can be viewed, rotated and edited instantly, so design changes are cheap, and a single parametric file can be shared by a team and reused to produce every derived drawing, cutting design time and cost. The model can also be analysed and simulated (stress, finite element analysis, CFD, interference and tolerance checks) before any material is cut, so fewer physical prototypes are needed and faults are found early. Finally it gives immediate outputs — 3D views, rendered images, hardcopy drawings and CNC data — with better accuracy and consistency than manual drafting.

CAD allows a number of immediate outputs such as a visual image, 3D representation and printed hardcopies as well as finite element analysis. It also allows drawings to be modified easily and shared as a collaborative file, with changes reflected across all related documents.

content.text: The photograph shows a board with a hydrofoil attached underneath. The hydrofoil is used to lift the board out of the water as the rider is towed behind a boat at high speed. Explain why the hydrofoil can lift the board out of the water when it is travelling at high speed.
The foil is an aerofoil, so use the pressure difference between its two surfaces to explain the direction of the force.
Remember the second contribution as well: the foil deflects water downwards, and the reaction to that deflection also acts upwards on the board.

Explain why the force is only large enough to lift the board at high speed — think about how much water the foil has to move each second as the board speeds up, and how the pressure difference depends on the flow speed.

As the board is towed forward, water flows over and around the hydrofoil. Because the foil is shaped like a wing, the water is deflected downwards and the flow over the upper surface speeds up, lowering the pressure above the foil relative to the pressure below it. The resultant of the higher pressure beneath and the lower pressure above is an upward lift, and the reaction to the downward momentum given to the water adds to it. The faster the board travels, the more water the foil must move each second and the greater the pressure difference, so the lift grows with the square of the speed. Above a critical speed the lift exceeds the weight of the board and rider and the board is lifted clear of the water.

As the board moves forwards the water flows over and around the hydrofoil. The shape of the hydrofoil, similar to an aircraft wing, creates a difference in pressure above and below the foil: low pressure above and higher pressure below. This difference means the higher pressure lifts the hydrofoil and therefore the board upwards. Lift is also created by the deflection of water downwards at the trailing edge. Above a critical speed the board is lifted out of the water.
